paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: you can bring God everything, and Psalm 86 shows it. David, Israel's king, walks in and says he is "poor and needy" (Psalm 86:1). No fancy speech, no polishing it up first. He calls on the Lord "all day long" (Psalm 86:3), and I'd say that's a man who is NOT going to hang up the call. You don't have to show up with your act together. You just have to show up.

Why can David pray like that? Because of who he says God is: "kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion to all who call on You" (Psalm 86:5). Even with ruthless men after him, he says God is "a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (Psalm 86:15). He doesn't pray like that because his day is going great. He prays that way because he knows the One he's talking to. Trouble can be loud, but it never gets to tell you what God is like.

And look at what David asks for in the middle of all that. He doesn't only ask to be rescued. He prays, "Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth. Give me an undivided heart" (Psalm 86:11). I want that too, friend, a heart that's all in and not half asleep. So bring God your needs, and then ask Him to teach you, because the One who answers your cry is also the One worth following.
